name: Zight
subcategory: screen recording, walkthroughs and product demos
tagline: Capture screen, GIF, or screenshot and create a shareable hosted link

pricing.notes: Typical Pro monthly rate; annual billing is lower.

tiers.name: Share
tiers.limits: Basic screenshot, GIF and screen-recording capture and hosted sharing; current numeric storage/item/length caps are not publicly disclosed

tiers.name: Create
tiers.limits: Advanced capture, editing, AI and individual sharing features
tiers.notes: Formerly called Pro. The supplied snapshot said $13.95/month; the current live monthly price is $12.95.

tiers.name: Collaborate
tiers.limits: Team collaboration, administration and shared-workspace features

tiers.name: Scale
tiers.limits: Custom seats, security, administration, support and procurement

pricing.freeTierCaps: permanent Share plan, but the current official pricing/help pages do not disclose numeric storage, recording-length or item caps
pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual; Create trial 7 days and Collaborate trial 14 days
pricing.hiddenCosts: Every paid user is a seat; team/workspace downgrades can require support, and the public page does not state overage pricing for hosted storage.

verdictSummary: The core loop is buildable, but a dependable replacement becomes a real weekend or multi-day project. For Zight, capture screen, GIF, or screenshot and create a shareable hosted link. The hard boundary is cloud storage, link management, viewer analytics, integrations, and team libraries, plus capture polish, hosting, and collaboration.
coreLoopDIY: Capture a screen recording, GIF, or screenshot with optional microphone audio, trim and annotate the result, and export a local file or create a shareable hosted link.
whatYouLose: cloud storage, link management, viewer analytics, integrations, and team libraries
ongoingBurden: OS permissions, codecs, rendering performance, uploads, storage, links, and viewer analytics
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Zight because the recording itself is easy; the subscription removes upload, transcoding, sharing, organization, and support work. The recurring cost buys OS permissions, codecs, rendering performance, uploads, storage, links, and viewer analytics, not just the visible interface.

priorArt.name: Cap
priorArt.desc: Open-source screen recording and sharing product with modern desktop architecture.

alternatives.name: Cap
alternatives.desc: Screen recordings and screenshots with hosted links; the self-hosted option comes with chores.

alternatives.name: ShareX
alternatives.desc: Screenshots, GIFs, recordings and upload links, wrapped in unapologetic Windows utility energy.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Pro plan and a personal desktop recorder DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Zight in an empty repository.
Use Tauri 2, React, TypeScript, ffmpeg, and SQLite; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: capture a screen recording, GIF, or screenshot with optional microphone audio, trim and annotate the result, and export a local file or create a shareable hosted link.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Offer screen, window, or region capture plus optional microphone audio.
Show an always-visible recording timer and make stop available from the tray.
Create a non-destructive trim view with crop, zoom, cursor highlight, and text callouts.
Render locally through ffmpeg with sensible H.264 and WebM presets.
Generate a poster frame, transcript, and Markdown summary beside each video.
Provide copy-file-path and reveal-in-folder actions instead of mandatory cloud upload.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out public cloud hosting.
Deliberately leave out viewer identity and engagement analytics.
Deliberately leave out enterprise workspaces and SSO.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
